seo_title: Cervicogenic Headache Treatment | North Palm Beach PT
seo_desc: Cervicogenic headache treatment in North Palm Beach. One-on-one physical therapy for the neck joints and muscles behind your headaches. Call 561-624-4263.
lede: Physical therapy for headaches that start in the neck, using hands-on care and targeted exercise to restore neck motion and reduce how often headaches return.
what_it_is: A cervicogenic headache is head pain that comes from a problem in your neck. Cleveland Clinic describes it as referred pain: you feel it in your head, but the source is in the bones, joints or soft tissues of the upper neck. StatPearls explains that nerves from the top three neck levels (C1 to C3) share a relay point in the brainstem with nerves from the face and head, so the brain can read neck pain as headache.

Cervicogenic headaches are less common than many other headache types. Cleveland Clinic reports that they affect between 0.4% and 4% of people who have headaches. Symptoms usually begin after age 30, though Cleveland Clinic notes many people do not seek care until their late 40s. Whiplash, arthritis and other neck injuries are common starting points.
symptoms: Headache on one side that starts at the base of the skull or in the neck
Pain that spreads toward the temple, forehead or behind the eye
Reduced neck movement, especially turning the head
Headaches set off or worsened by neck movement or certain neck positions
Tender muscles at the back of the head on the painful side
Neck pain alongside the headache, though not in every case
causes: Arthritis in the joints of the upper neck
A herniated or slipped disc in the neck
A pinched nerve in the neck
Long periods of slouched or forward-head posture

how_therapy_helps.intro: Cleveland Clinic notes that many people find success managing these headaches with physical therapy. The 2017 neck pain clinical practice guideline in the Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy recommends that, for chronic neck pain with headache, clinicians combine cervical or cervicothoracic mobilization or manipulation with stretching, strengthening and endurance exercise for the neck and shoulder girdle. Treatment targets the neck problem that is feeding the headache.
methods: Gentle, skilled hands-on techniques to the stiff upper neck joints aim to restore motion and reduce the pain signal that refers into the head.
The JOSPT guideline supports a C1 to C2 self-SNAG, a towel-assisted rotation exercise you can repeat at home to keep the top of the neck moving.
Exercises for the deep neck muscles build the endurance needed to hold your head comfortably through a workday.
Stretching and strengthening the upper back and shoulder blade muscles, as the guideline recommends, reduces strain on the neck.
Your therapist reviews how you sit, drive and use screens, and suggests adjustments that limit the positions that bring on your headaches.

first_visit: Your first visit lasts about an hour. Your therapist asks about your headache pattern, where the pain starts, what neck positions or activities set it off, and screens for warning signs that point to another cause. The 2017 JOSPT guideline recommends measuring active neck range of motion, performing the cervical flexion-rotation test and checking upper neck joint mobility. Posture and shoulder blade strength are assessed as well. Treatment and a home program begin that day.
recovery: Response to treatment varies. Cleveland Clinic notes that headaches can feel worse when physical therapy begins, and that your therapist paces exercise to limit this. Cleveland Clinic also cites one study in which 72% of people had at least 50% fewer headaches 12 months after starting physical therapy. Results like these are not guaranteed, and long-standing headaches or older injuries may take more time, so consistent home exercise is part of the plan.
self_care: Set up your desk and screen so you are not craning your head forward
Use a pillow that supports the natural curve of your neck
Take short breaks to move your neck and shoulders during long tasks
Stay regularly active with exercise you enjoy
Keep a simple log of neck positions or activities that come before each headache
see_a_doctor: A sudden, explosive or violent headache (call 911)
A headache that feels like the worst of your life
Headache with trouble speaking, vision changes, confusion, loss of balance, or weakness in an arm or leg
Headache with fever, a stiff neck, nausea and vomiting
A headache that follows a head injury
New headaches that begin after age 50

faqs.q: How do I know if my headache is coming from my neck?
faqs.a: Cervicogenic headaches usually affect one side, start at the base of the skull or in the neck, and spread forward toward the temple or eye. Cleveland Clinic notes they often come with limited neck movement and get worse when you move your neck. A physical exam that tests neck motion and the upper neck joints helps confirm whether the neck is the source.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a cervicogenic headache and a migraine?
faqs.a: A migraine is a primary headache, meaning it is a condition of its own. Cleveland Clinic classifies cervicogenic headache as a secondary headache, caused by an underlying problem in the neck. Cervicogenic headaches tend to stay on one side, follow neck movement or posture and come with reduced neck motion. The two can overlap, so a physician should evaluate unclear or changing headache patterns.

faqs.q: Can poor posture cause cervicogenic headaches?
faqs.a: Posture can contribute. The APTA ChoosePT headache guide lists poor posture, fatigue and stress among factors in neck-related headaches, and Cleveland Clinic recommends good posture, avoiding slouching and using a supportive pillow as prevention. Sustained forward-head positions load the upper neck joints and muscles. Posture changes work best combined with neck and shoulder exercise.

faqs.q: Can a physical therapist help headaches caused by the neck?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Cleveland Clinic notes that many people find success managing cervicogenic headaches with physical therapy. The 2017 JOSPT neck pain guideline recommends joint mobilization or manipulation combined with neck and shoulder girdle stretching, strengthening and endurance exercise for chronic neck pain with headache. A physical therapist evaluates your neck and builds a plan around those findings.

It can. Cleveland Clinic lists whiplash among the injuries and conditions of the cervical spine that can lead to cervicogenic headache. Any headache after a car accident or blow to the head should first be checked by a physician to rule out other injuries before neck rehabilitation begins.

faqs.q: Do cervicogenic headaches show up on an MRI?
faqs.a: Not always. Cleveland Clinic explains that X-rays, CT scans or MRIs can identify structural neck problems, but a normal scan does not rule out the neck as the source of your headache. Diagnosis relies heavily on your history and physical exam, matched against criteria from the International Classification of Headache Disorders.

signOrSymptom: one-sided headache starting at the base of the skull

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 G44.86 (Cervicogenic headache) verified as billable on icd10data.com; its 'code also' note asks for any associated cervical spinal condition.
The JOSPT 2017 CPG recommends 'manipulation or mobilization'. The page leads with mobilization; confirm whether our therapists perform cervical thrust manipulation before adding it.
The 72% figure is cited from StatPearls (and also appears on Cleveland Clinic). It comes from a single trial (likely Jull et al., 2002); framed as one study with no promise.

The ChoosePT headache guide calls cervicogenic headaches 'muscle-spasm headaches' and 'the most common types of headaches in adults', which conflicts with the 0.4% to 4% figure from Cleveland Clinic and StatPearls. That claim was not used; ChoosePT is cited only for posture, stress and workstation factors.
The C1-2 self-SNAG is described as 'towel-assisted'; the guideline names the exercise but not the towel method. Confirm wording.
Migraine comparison FAQ uses general primary vs secondary headache definitions from Cleveland Clinic; clinician may want to review.

Fact-check: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) could not be fetched during fact-check (reCAPTCHA block). Number and effectiveness claims were re-attributed to Cleveland Clinic and JOSPT; the C1 to C3 relay-point explanation and the 'tender muscles at the back of the head' symptom still rest on StatPearls and were not re-verified.
